planting.note: Plant container stock into acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; this vigorous species tolerates deeper shade than most garden rhododendrons but flowers more heavily with some filtered sun.

directions: Native to the mountain forests of the Iberian Peninsula, the western Caucasus, and the Pontic region of the Black Sea coast, this large evergreen species produces dense trusses of lavender-pink flowers in late spring against glossy, leathery foliage. Its vigor and tolerance of poor, acidic soils made it a mainstay rootstock and woodland garden shrub in Western horticulture for over two centuries, though gardeners in the British Isles and Pacific Northwest should site it thoughtfully since it self-seeds readily into open woodland there. Give it room to spread into a substantial mounded shrub and avoid alkaline or waterlogged soils, which it tolerates poorly. Light pruning after flowering keeps size in check without sacrificing next year's bloom.

planting.note: Plant in gritty, well-drained soil amended with leaf mold; unlike most rhododendrons this alpine species tolerates lime and does not require strictly acidic conditions.

directions: Found on limestone cliffs and rocky slopes throughout the European Alps, this low, densely branched evergreen shrublet is distinguished from its lookalike neighbor Rhododendron ferrugineum by bristly, ciliate leaf margins and its unusual tolerance for calcareous soils. Clusters of small, rose-pink, bell-shaped flowers appear in early summer, held just above the tidy dark foliage. It needs sharp drainage and resents summer heat and humidity, making it best suited to rock gardens, raised beds, or cool mountain climates rather than lowland borders. Water during dry spells but never let the crown sit wet through winter.

planting.note: Plant in a gritty, humus-rich, moisture-retentive but sharply drained mix; this circumboreal dwarf resents hot, dry summers far more than cold winters.

directions: This deciduous dwarf rhododendron hugs the ground across its circumboreal range, from the Kamchatka Peninsula and northern Japan to the Aleutians and coastal Alaska, where it grows in tundra and subalpine turf. In late spring it produces disproportionately large, flat, rose-purple flowers relative to its tiny creeping stature, making it a favorite curiosity among alpine and rock garden collectors. It demands cool roots, reliable moisture, and excellent drainage, performing best in troughs or raised beds in climates with cool summers. Avoid any mulch or soil that stays soggy in winter, since crown rot is the most common cause of loss in cultivation.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (NARGS) Seed Exchange

planting.note: Plant in acidic, peaty, evenly moist soil with cool root conditions; a classic cool-summer alpine species that struggles in hot, humid lowland gardens.

directions: One of the first rhododendron species known to European botanists, this low evergreen shrub was collected from the mountains of Siberia, Sakhalin, Korea, and Japan, where it forms sprawling mats in subalpine and alpine tundra. Pale yellow, funnel-shaped flowers open in small clusters just after snowmelt, a color still uncommon among hardy rhododendron species. It thrives only where summers stay cool, so it is best grown at elevation or in northern climates in a peaty, acidic bed with constant but never stagnant moisture. Protect the shallow root mat with a light organic mulch going into winter in exposed sites.

planting.note: Plant container stock into acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light shade; among the more cold-tolerant wild camellia species, it has been used as a breeding parent for hardier hybrids.

directions: Native to the mountain forests of western China, this slender-leaved species takes its name from the narrow, tapering, spine-tipped foliage that distinguishes it from the broader-leaved camellias more familiar in gardens. Small, single white flowers with a boss of yellow stamens open in autumn, set against airy, open growth that gives the shrub a more delicate look than Camellia japonica. Its relative cold tolerance has made it a useful parent in breeding programs aimed at expanding camellia hardiness into colder zones. Grow it as an understory shrub with dappled light and consistent moisture, and shelter it from harsh winter wind in its coldest hardiness zones.

planting.note: Plant container stock into acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in filtered shade; this species is more cold-sensitive than sasanqua camellias and benefits from a sheltered site.

directions: Collected from the hill forests along the Yunnan-Guangxi border and into northern Vietnam, this little-grown species produces an airy cascade of small, single white flowers along arching branches in mid to late autumn. Its loose, graceful habit and slender willowy branches give it a more informal silhouette than most garden camellias, making it popular among species collectors for woodland plantings. It wants steady moisture and filtered light rather than the fuller sun tolerated by sasanqua types, and its somewhat tender nature calls for a protected microclimate at the cold edge of its range. Light shaping after flowering keeps the naturally twiggy growth from becoming congested.

planting.note: Plant container stock into acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; fragrance is strongest on mild, still autumn days.

directions: Native to the limestone hills of Guangxi, China, this species bears small, single white flowers with a notably strong, sweet fragrance that opens in autumn and persists over a long bloom season. Fine-textured, narrow leaves give the shrub a soft, airy texture distinct from the bolder foliage of japonica types, and it has drawn interest from breeders seeking fragrance genes for hardier hybrid camellias. Grow it in humus-rich, acidic soil with reliable moisture and partial shade, siting it near a path or entry where the scent can be appreciated. It tolerates light frost but appreciates wind shelter in its coldest hardiness range.
